batches.title: Choose where an account's data lives
features: Data residency (choice of region per account)
batches.brief: Needs self-host. Goal: one product, several servers, each in a region; an account lives on the one it chose. 1. Each server has REGION_NAME and knows the others through REGION_DIRECTORY (name, country and base URL of each, the same on all). 2. Sign-up asks where the account's data should live (suggested from the browser's time zone, never chosen silently); the account is made on that server. 3. A small shared lookup (email hash to region, nothing else) lets the login page send people to their server; it is the only thing kept outside the region, and the pages say so. 4. Signing links, emails and /verify already use the server's own address; envelope IDs get a region prefix so /verify elsewhere can say 'try <region>'. 5. /security on each server lists what leaves its region (mail, texts, payments, model) from src/lib/dataplace.ts. Tests (tests/regions.test.ts): two servers in one test (two data folders), sign-up on each, login routing through the lookup, the verify hint, nothing but the email hash in the lookup. Leave out: moving an account between regions. House rules: read before editing, re-read before each edit (others edit too); in shared files (sign page, envelopes.ts, pdf.ts, settings page, db.ts, openapi.ts, README) small edits only, never reformat, logic in your own modules; tables and columns appended in db.ts; new route files imported in src/app/api/[...path]/route.ts and in openapi.ts; settings in .env.example; new words through t() once lang-core is in; plain words, no em dashes; check 390 and 320 px; npm test and npm run typecheck pass; README says exactly what was built.
batches.needs_from_operator: Hosting in each region, and a mail provider per region where mail must stay in region.

batches.title: Keys the customer holds
features: Customer-controlled encryption keys
batches.brief: Needs db-encrypt. 1. An account can wrap its own data key with a key in its own key service (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, or HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao transit), set by its admin with the key's identifier and the credentials the account gives (stored encrypted). 2. The account's files and encrypted columns use its data key; the server unwraps it through the customer's service and keeps it in memory for at most CMK_CACHE_MINUTES. 3. If the customer revokes the key, the account's documents cannot be opened: signing pages and the app say 'The documents of <organisation> cannot be opened right now because their key is not available.' and nothing is lost. 4. Words: 'Our server still decrypts documents to show and sign them. Revoking the key stops that.' Never 'we cannot read your documents'. Tests (tests/cmk.test.ts): a stub transit service, unwrap and cache, revoke stops reads with the message, restore. Leave out: keys per envelope. House rules: read before editing, re-read before each edit (others edit too); in shared files (sign page, envelopes.ts, pdf.ts, settings page, db.ts, openapi.ts, README) small edits only, never reformat, logic in your own modules; tables and columns appended in db.ts; new route files imported in src/app/api/[...path]/route.ts and in openapi.ts; settings in .env.example; new words through t() once lang-core is in; plain words, no em dashes; check 390 and 320 px; npm test and npm run typecheck pass; README says exactly what was built.
batches.needs_from_operator: The customer's own key service.

left_out.name: Knowledge-based authentication (KBA)
left_out.why: Questions drawn from public and commercial records are weak (NIST SP 800-63B forbids them as an authenticator), US only, and need a credit-bureau contract with a permissible-purpose review. Offering it would claim more strength than it has. id-login and id-docs cover identity honestly.

left_out.name: Our own identity wallet
left_out.why: Holding verified identities makes us a far bigger target and a controller of sensitive data. Accept the EU Digital Identity Wallet and reusable identities through brokers in id-login instead.

left_out.name: Reading ID card or passport chips (NFC)
left_out.why: Browsers cannot read passport or ID chips (Web NFC reads only NDEF tags), so an installable web app cannot. Providers in id-docs do it in their own apps.

left_out.name: Native store apps for iOS and Android
left_out.why: Replaced by the installable web app (phone-app), as the rules ask. Store apps need developer accounts and review cycles; phone-app lists what a web app cannot do (no store listing, no chip reading, no notifications, no share target on iPhone).

left_out.name: Remote online notarisation with our own video platform
left_out.why: US only, state-by-state registration, an audio-video recording kept 10 years, credential analysis and KBA. The notary batch hands off to a licensed partner and supports a notary in the room instead.

left_out.name: Becoming a Qualified Trust Service Provider
left_out.why: Needs conformity assessment by an accredited body, supervision, insurance, HSMs and audits at least every 24 months. Not sensible for this team; qtsp partners with one.

left_out.name: Country-specific certificate signatures (ICP-Brasil, India eSign, Mexico NOM 151)
left_out.why: One contract with a licensed provider per country. The CSC client in qtsp is the base; add a country only when a real customer asks.

left_out.name: A platform-issued certificate per signature (like DocuSign's ds_email)
left_out.why: Adds little over the document seal (seal) and certificates from our own CA could be mistaken for advanced signatures.

left_out.name: Authoritative copy and eVault for transferable records
left_out.why: Needs a custodian design under UETA section 16 and ESIGN section 201, usually a specialist custodian; not something small organisations or our public bodies need. Never claim a document is an authoritative copy.

left_out.name: Blockchain anchoring of agreements
left_out.why: Proves no more than an RFC 3161 time-stamp of the audit chain head (seal-ltv), needs a funded wallet run by the operator, and risks putting personal data on a public chain.

left_out.name: Premium data verification fields (SSN, FEIN, bank accounts against outside databases)
left_out.why: US-centred paid services that differ per country, low value for our users. fields-checks checks formats and says it checks the format only.

left_out.name: A UK Right to Work workflow sold as such
left_out.why: Only a check by a certified identity service provider counts. id-docs lets an employer use a certified provider; we never label our own flow certified.

left_out.name: Vendor signature pad SDKs (Topaz, ePad, IntegriSign)
left_out.why: They need drivers on each counter computer and tie us to vendors. Pen tablets that act as a pointer already work on the draw pad.

left_out.name: Document markup by signers (white-out, adding text)
left_out.why: Comments plus the sender's Correct with the sign-again rule cover the need; letting signers rewrite wording invites disputes about which text was agreed.

left_out.name: Raising limits to DocuSign's (99 recipients, 2,000 pages, 999-day deadline, 50-member groups)
left_out.why: Our limits come from what a phone can open and from keeping reminders and daily limits sane. Raise one when a customer needs it.

left_out.name: Switching off the envelope ID on pages, or a movable envelope ID field
left_out.why: The ID on every page is what /verify?id and holders of printed copies rely on.

left_out.name: Renewing archive time-stamps over the years (PAdES B-LTA renewal)
left_out.why: Each renewal changes the file everyone holds and its fingerprint, which /verify and the emails depend on. seal-ltv adds B-LT and one archive time-stamp at completion.

left_out.name: Reading zones drawn by the sender for screen readers
left_out.why: Few senders would draw them. The reflowed reading view and text from scanned pages (reading-view, a11y) cover most of the need.

left_out.name: A watched 24/7 security monitoring service
left_out.why: Needs people. sec-log keeps the record, sends alerts and exports to the customer's own security system; watching it is the customer's or operator's job.

left_out.name: Security certifications themselves (ISO 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP, GovRAMP, DoD IL4, IRAP, G-Cloud)
left_out.why: They need an audit firm or accredited assessor, often a sponsoring agency and authorised hosting. self-host builds the software and documents an auditor asks for; never claim a certification or 'alignment'.

left_out.name: US PIV and CAC smart cards
left_out.why: They need middleware on the signer's computer. webeid covers EU national ID cards; revisit when a US agency asks.

left_out.name: Smart sections as a separate feature (rotating tables, collapsed terms)
left_out.why: Folded into reading-view, without collapsing terms at the start, because collapsed text is still what is signed.

left_out.name: Expiring signatures, the 10-trees note and first-time animation, and the AI chat helper
left_out.why: Already briefed separately (research/briefs.json keys 'expiry', 'impact' and 'chat') and owned by other engineers; not repeated here. ai-assist and ai-repo build on the chat helper's provider module.

plan.notes:
How this plan was made. I read README.md 'What is in it' and 'What is not in it' and checked the inventory's claims in the code, read only (no files changed; no scratch files were needed). The README matches the code with these differences. (1) Stamps are built, as the critic said: 'stamp' is in FIELD_TYPES (src/server/envelopes.ts:42), and README's field editor list (line 216) still leaves Stamp out. (2) The locale columns on users, recipients and envelopes exist in src/server/db.ts and nothing uses them, so lang-core can start from them. (3) Access codes are stored as typed (recipients.access_code) and compared with safeEqual (src/server/routes-sign.ts:210); id-small hashes them. (4) There is no manifest or service worker in public/; next.config.mjs sends X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN and frame-ancestors 'self' except for click-to-agree embeds. (5) storeUpload accepts only PDF, PNG and JPEG (routes-envelopes.ts:53). (6) No send_at, custom fields, visibility, supplements, BCC, retention, OCR, PDF/A, PAdES or security event log exist (grep). (7) Passwords need only 8 characters (routes-account.ts:91, 261, 355); two-step can already be required by the owner (accounts.two_step_required_at). (8) credits.ts line 7 still says signatures never expire; the expiry brief (research/briefs.json key 'expiry') owns that change. (9) buildFinal in envelopes.ts is the single place the signed file is made and hashed, so the seal batch adds src/server/finalpipe.ts there and pdfa, eseal, qtsp and visibility join it. (10) cron.ts is 38 lines and the settings page adds a tab with one line per component (as StampSettings does), so batches touch those files with one-line hooks.

Order and waves. The batches are listed in a sensible start order. Wave 1, can start now in parallel (distinct files): lang-core, convert, seal, mail-records, templates-lib, sec-log, retention, custom-fields, channels, self-host, reports, phone-app, db-encrypt (coordinate its envelopes.ts edits). Wave 2: lang-signing and lang-mail (after lang-core); seal-ltv, pdfa, eseal (after seal); sec-policy (after sec-log); page-tools and cloud-pick (after convert). Wave 3, after lang-signing, all small edits to the signing page: consent-own, paper, id-small, timing, fields-checks, a11y, preview, switches, supplements, visibility (also after seal), witness-two, delegate, reading-view, qtsp (also after seal); sso-oidc after sec-policy, then id-login, part11 and sso-saml-scim. Wave 4: lang-first, lang-sender, lang-sender-rest; fields-kinds, collab-fields; routing-if then recipient-types; web-forms; pay-collect; dev-api; offline-inperson; id-docs; webeid; colleagues; perm-profiles; tpl-combine; notary; ai-assist and ai-repo (after the separate chat helper); regions; cmk. Languages come first because nearly every later batch adds sentences; after lang-core every new sentence goes through t(). The converter comes before Word upload, page tools and cloud pickers; the seal pipeline before PDF/A, organisation seals, qualified signatures and per-person copies.

Value for small organisations and public bodies, highest first: languages; Word upload; the seal readable in Acrobat; archive copies of emails (records and freedom of information); retention with legal holds; case numbers (custom fields); WhatsApp; sign on paper; ready-made templates; the security record; accessibility; the account's own consent text; single sign-on; self-hosting in one's own country; PDF/A. These are also what public procurement usually asks for (accessibility statement, SSO, audit export, retention schedules, data location, archive formats), which the next step of the owner's request (why governments have not adopted DocuSign widely) can build on.

House rules for every engineer (each brief carries a short form): read each file before changing it and again before each edit, because many engineers edit at the same time. In the busiest shared files (src/app/sign/[token]/page.tsx, src/server/envelopes.ts, src/server/pdf.ts, src/app/app/settings/page.tsx, src/server/db.ts, src/server/openapi.ts, README.md) make small edits only, never reformat, and put the logic in your own new modules. New tables go at the end of SCHEMA and new columns at the end of COLUMNS in db.ts. A new route file is imported in src/app/api/[...path]/route.ts and described in openapi.ts; every setting goes in .env.example. Never touch src/server/routes-billing.ts or src/server/credits.ts (the payment owner's); ask them when a feature uses or returns a signature, and use the existing completion and return paths. The product is being renamed growsigning: write the name through one constant, never a new literal 'Sign&Grow'. Plain words, no em dashes. Check screens at 390 and 320 px and on a desktop. npm test and npm run typecheck pass. README says exactly what was built and what was not. Do not attach or move any domain: CLAUDE.md at the repository root forbids attaching treegens.app and the other listed domains to any Netlify site. All paths are relative to /home/user/treegens-app/sign-and-grow.

Money and trees. Features that cost per use at an outside provider (WhatsApp, phone calls, ID checks, logins at identity brokers, qualified signatures, notarisation, the AI model) stay off for accounts until the owner sets a price in src/lib/impact.ts that covers the provider's cost and the planting share; every plan keeps paying for mangroves. The '10 mangroves' line follows the impact brief's rule (only for a paid signature). Paper signing, delegates and certificate signers use a signature through the existing completion path, so the tree line applies to them unchanged.

Tools on this machine for tests: openssl, pdfsig (poppler), Java and LibreOffice are installed; Tesseract and veraPDF are not, so those tests skip when missing.

Research caveat carried from the inventory: DocuSign's own pages could not be fetched from this session; DocuSign facts come from search summaries, and plan tiers often disagree between DocuSign pages. Briefs never depend on a DocuSign tier.
